title: Can, want, must, may
goal: Build two-verb sentences with helper verbs and the *-ni* infinitive — the structure behind most adult conversation.

notes: **The Hungarian infinitive always ends in -ni.** *segít* → *segíteni*, *csinál* → *csinálni*, *néz* → *nézni*, *ír* → *írni*. It follows a helper verb, just like "to …" or the bare verb in English after "can", "want to", "must".
**Tudsz segíteni? is the most natural way to ask for help.** Literally "can you help?". The polite form is *Tudna segíteni?* — with a softened helper verb, just like *szeretnék* in unit 7.

**Meg tudom nézni** shows two important things at once. First, the prefix (*meg-*) jumps to the **front of the whole phrase**, separated from its verb. Second, the helper verb takes the **definite** form (*tudom*, not *tudok*), because the object in question — the form — is already clear.

**Ki kell töltenem** is *kell* with a person. The infinitive takes a possessive ending: *töltenem* (I fill), *töltened* (you fill), *töltenie* (he/she fills). It sounds complicated but it's used constantly, so it's worth recognizing now even before you build it yourself.
**Mit kell csinálni? is impersonal kell.** Nobody says who has to do it — just like "what needs to be done?" in English. This form is shorter and always safe, so use it first.
**Lehet means both "may" and "maybe".** *Le lehet adni* = "it can be handed in". *Lehet* also works on its own as an answer: *Lehet.* = "You may" or "Maybe", depending on the tone of voice.

grammars.title: Helper verb + infinitive
body: The pattern is always the same: the helper verb changes with the person, the infinitive never changes.

head: Magyar
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: *Itt lehet dohányozni?* = Can I smoke here?

after: **Tud has two jobs.** It means "can" with an infinitive (*tudok úszni* — I can swim), and "know" with an object (*tudom a választ* — I know the answer). For languages: *tudok magyarul* = I can speak Hungarian.
**Akar sounds firmer than you'd think.** *Akarok* is a bit blunt — for polite requests use *szeretnék*. The difference is the same as *I want* versus *I would like*.
**Lehet and szabad never change.** Both are impersonal, so their form is always the same, whatever happens around them.

grammars.title: Kell: with and without a person
body: Two patterns, both correct, used for two slightly different purposes.
after: The impersonal form is used for general rules: *Itt fizetni kell* (you pay here). The personal form is used when the person matters: *Mennem kell* (I have to go) — a sentence you'll say often when taking your leave.

If you're not ready for the personal form yet, there's a perfectly correct way out: name the person with *nekem*, *neked*, and so on, then use the plain *-ni* form. *Nekem tanulni kell* is understood perfectly, just slightly less neat.

grammars.title: Where does the prefix go?
body: The rule from unit 12, now with one more situation.

head: Situation
Prefix position
Example
rows: attached to the front of the verb

after: The last row trips up beginners most, because the result looks like three unrelated words: *le lehet adni*, *meg tudom nézni*, *fel kell hívni*. Accept it as one chunk; your ear will get used to it faster than your logic.
If you're really unsure, a sentence without the prefix is almost always still understood. A misplaced prefix marks you as a beginner, but it never makes your sentence fail.

blocks.text: *Segíthetek?* contains the infix *-hat/-het*, meaning "may" or "can". It goes right inside the verb: *ír* → *írhat* (may write), *megy* → *mehet* (may go), *kér* → *kérhet* (may ask). It's very typically Hungarian and very useful; at A1 just recognize it, at A2 you'll use it every day.

sections.title: At the office: forms and official business

blocks.title: Three lifesaving sentences at the counter
items: *Elnézést, hol kell sorszámot húzni?* — "Excuse me, where do I take a queue number?" Almost every Hungarian office uses a ticket machine, and standing in the wrong line can cost you an hour.
*Beszél angolul valaki?* — "Does anyone speak English?" Honest and effective; in big offices there usually is someone.
*Le tudná írni?* — "Could you write it down?" Getting the answer in writing is much safer than relying on an untrained ear.
